title: What’s the Secret to Bats’ Super Longevity? - Nautilus
gist: A Nature study of Myotis bats suggests their exceptional disease resistance and long lifespans—driven partly by multiple copies of immune proteins that repair cell damage—may be shaped together by evolution rather than as separate traits.

insights.claim: The largest bat genus, Myotis, can carry up to hundreds of viruses without getting sick, and the tiny Brandt's bat can live as long as 42 years relative to its minuscule body size.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: These extreme traits make bats a model system for aging and immunity research relevant to human health.
insights.locator: can carry up to hundreds of viruses without ever getting sick

insights.claim: Multiple copies of immune proteins give Myotis bats an edge in fixing cell damage, according to a Nature study of their genes.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Points to a specific genetic mechanism that could inform longevity and immunity science.
insights.locator: Multiples of immune proteins give them an edge

themes.theme: Linked evolution of aging and immunity

insights.claim: Pathogen resistance and longevity are usually studied as separate biological problems, but the bat results suggest evolution may be shaping them together, per co-lead author Elise Lauterbur.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Reframes aging and immunity as potentially coupled, a non-obvious angle for longevity research.
insights.quote: These are often studied as separate biological problems. But our results suggest that evolution may be shaping them together.
insights.locator: explained co-lead study author Elise Lauterbur
